summary:
Niger State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which reaches into every part of the state. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide and extends well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

A second, state-level layer applies in Niger State specifically. Human Rights Watch (2004) documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria and lists the twelve states concerned: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. The wave traces from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000, and the provisions remain in force. The UK Home Office note records Sharia law in all twelve states as criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Niger State enacted its own statutory machinery for that layer. The Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000) was signed into law on 22 February 2000 and came into operation on 4 May 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36). It is a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein. The enactment defines adultery to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher punishment specified by Sharia, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68; the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies.

The editor of Ostien's sourcebook notes that the 2000 enactment is not a complete Sharia Penal Code. It amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and the text is reproduced in full. The UK Home Office note sets out Nigeria's hybrid legal system, the twelve-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women.

The consequence for a visitor is a parallel track that operates independently of federal law. A Muslim visitor who is outed in Niger State stands under a harsher legal frame than the national statute alone imposes, because religion and the standard of proof determine which punishment applies to the same conduct. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
The Sharia layer in Niger State is one instance of a wider northern-bloc pattern rather than a local anomaly. Human Rights Watch (2004) records the adoption wave across twelve named states over 1999 and 2000, so the same second layer is present in neighbouring states and absent from the south. A visitor who crosses state lines inside Nigeria changes which criminal track applies in addition to the national statute, which does not vary by location.

The two layers are built differently. The national Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies uniformly regardless of the defendant's religion, while Niger State's amendment turns on religious identity and evidentiary standard, so identical conduct can attract different burdens of proof and different penalties within the same state. The UK Home Office note describes the resulting system as hybrid.

The state provision is an amendment to a pre-existing colonial-era code rather than a stand-alone religious statute, which is why the ordinary Penal Code punishment continues to apply in default. The 2000 law's own text and its legislative history are publicly reproduced in Ostien's sourcebook, making the operative wording verifiable at source.
localsOnly:
Niger State residents operate under three overlapping instruments: the federal Penal Code as amended by the state's Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, the Sharia layer available for Muslim defendants under section 68A, and the national Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014. The state Penal Code Law Cap 94 remains the base instrument; the 2000 amendment revised punishments within it and inserted the religious-identity provision rather than replacing it.

For a Muslim resident, a listed offence proved to the Islamic evidentiary standard attracts the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68. For a non-Muslim resident, or where the Islamic standard of proof is not met, the ordinary Penal Code punishment applies. Religion therefore functions as a determinant of penalty for the same act.

Adultery as defined in the amended state code includes sodomy, which brings same-sex conduct within the reach of the state's own criminal provisions alongside the national statute. Residents are additionally exposed to the national act's bans on cohabitation between same-sex partners, public display of a same-sex amorous relationship and operation of gay organisations, and to police use of that act to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.
outOfScopeNotes:
Arrest and prosecution figures for Niger State under section 68A are not available in the sources assembled here; the UK Home Office country policy and information note (version 4.0, June 2025) expressly records limits in the available arrest data. Whether the amended provisions have actually been applied in a reported same-sex conduct case in Niger State is therefore unresolved rather than established either way.

The full list of offences captured by the phrase 'a listed offence' in section 68A is not reproduced in the source inventory beyond the definition of adultery to include sodomy; the operative wording is available in the reproduced gazette text but the complete enumeration has not been verified here.

Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, reported by Reuters in September 2022, have been enacted is not settled by the sources available for this record. The status of the maximum-security placement question raised in the 2024 Bobrisky proceedings likewise turns on the national Correctional Service framework and is not a Niger State matter.
